name: Circadian rhythm
seoDesc: Circadian rhythm: work out next cycles' length from the sleep time1 and the sleep time3. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: The Circadian rhythm calculator turns the sleep time1 and the sleep time3 into next cycles' length. That makes it useful for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Circadian rhythm calculator work?
sections.html:
The Circadian rhythm calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports next cycles' length in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the waking up time); then you type in the sleep time1, the sleep time3 and the sleep time6.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Circadian rhythm calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Next cycles' length=-1 ÷ 5 × time to fall asleep − 1 ÷ 5 × first sleep cycle's length − 1 ÷ 5 × sleep time6 + (1 ÷ 5) × waking up time
Sleep time 5=-time to fall asleep − first sleep cycle's length − 4 × next cycles' length + waking up time
Sleep time 4=-time to fall asleep − first sleep cycle's length − 3 × next cycles' length + waking up time
Next cycles' length=-1 ÷ 2 × time to fall asleep − 1 ÷ 2 × first sleep cycle's length − 1 ÷ 2 × sleep time3 + (1 ÷ 2) × waking up time
Next cycles' length=-time to fall asleep − first sleep cycle's length − sleep time2 + waking up time
First sleep cycle's length=-time to fall asleep − sleep time1 + waking up time

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Circadian rhythm calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the sleep time1, the sleep time3 and the sleep time6 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Circadian rhythm calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns next cycles' length, derived from the sleep time1, the sleep time3 and the sleep time6. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Circadian rhythm calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the sleep time1, the sleep time3 and the sleep time6, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Circadian rhythm calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
